section.title: Pharaoh as a Fallen Cedar
section.sectionRationale: The oracles against Egypt near their close with an extended parable: Assyria pictured as the tallest, most beautiful cedar in Eden's own garden, admired by every nation, yet felled by ruthless foreigners and cast down to Sheol for the pride of its height. Ezekiel turns this warning directly on Pharaoh, closing the book's long sequence against human pride with its most vivid image yet.
section.thesis: Every greatness that forgets its Giver and climbs on its own pride is cut down, however tall it grows; Pharaoh is warned by Assyria's fall that his own splendor will end the same way, in the pit with the uncircumcised slain.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the tallest cedar in Eden's garden, unrivaled by any tree; its pride and its felling by a ruthless ruler; and its descent to Sheol, with the allegory turned directly on Pharaoh.

units.label: The tallest cedar in Eden
units.note: Assyria's unrivaled greatness, a warning held up to Pharaoh

verses.text: In the eleventh year, on the first day of the third month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: 
‘Who can be compared to your greatness?
Look at Assyria, a {{erez|cedar}} in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest. It towered on high; its top was among the clouds.
The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall, directing their streams all around its base and sending their channels to all the trees of the field.
Therefore it towered higher than all the trees of the field. Its branches multiplied, and its boughs grew long as it spread them out because of the abundant waters.
All the birds of the air nested in its branches, and all the beasts of the field gave birth beneath its boughs; all the great nations lived in its shade.
It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its limbs, for its roots extended to abundant waters.

The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it; the cypresses could not compare with its branches, nor the plane trees match its boughs. No tree in the garden of God could compare with its beauty.

I made it beautiful with its many branches, the envy of all the trees of Eden, 
which were in the garden of God.’

units.label: Cut down for its pride
units.note: judgment on a height that forgot its Giver

verses.text: Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Since it became great in {{gobah|height}} and set its top among the clouds, and it grew proud on account of its height,
I delivered it into the hand of the ruler of the nations, for him to deal with it according to its wickedness. I have banished it.

Foreigners, the most ruthless of the nations, cut it down and left it. Its branches have fallen on the mountains and in every valley; its boughs lay broken in all the earth's ravines. And all the peoples of the earth left its shade and abandoned it.
All the birds of the air nested on its fallen trunk, and all the beasts of the field lived among its boughs.

This happened so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height and set their tops among the clouds, and no other well-watered trees would reach them in height. For they have all been consigned to death, to the depths of the earth, among the mortals who descend to the Pit.’

units.label: Brought down to Sheol, this is Pharaoh
units.note: mourning, the pit, and the point of the whole allegory

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘On the day it was brought down to {{sheol|Sheol}}, I caused mourning. I covered the deep because of it; I held back its rivers; its abundant waters were restrained. I made Lebanon mourn for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it.

I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who descend to the Pit. 
Then all the trees of Eden, the choicest and best of Lebanon, all the well-watered trees, were consoled in the earth below.
They too descended with it to Sheol, to those slain by the sword. As its allies they had lived in its shade among the nations.

Who then is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden. You will lie among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD.’”

erez.gloss: Cedar, the tallest and most prized tree of the ancient world, especially the cedars of Lebanon. Chosen here because nothing pictured unrivaled greatness like a Lebanon cedar.

gobah.gloss: Height, but the same root gives rise to Hebrew words for haughtiness and arrogance. The tree's literal height and its pride are bound together in a single word.

sheol.gloss: Sheol, the shadowy realm of the dead. The tallest tree that ever grew and the proudest king who ever reigned both end up in the same low place.

basic.context: This closes the long sequence of oracles against Egypt with a vivid parable. Assyria is pictured as the tallest, most beautiful cedar that ever grew, envied by every tree in Eden's own garden, yet cut down by ruthless foreigners and cast into Sheol for the pride of its height. Ezekiel turns the warning directly on Pharaoh: what happened to proud Assyria will happen to proud Egypt too.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real prophetic oracle told through an extended botanical allegory, a device also used in Daniel 4's tree and Judges 9's parable of the trees. Its point is not botanical but moral and theological: greatness that forgets the Giver and exalts itself invites judgment, whatever nation wears the crown at the time.
basic.originalLanguages: The cedar is erez, the tallest, most prized tree in the ancient world. Its ruin comes because it 'became great in gobah', height, the very root behind Hebrew words for haughtiness; height and pride share one word. And its destination is Sheol, the shadowy realm of the dead, where every proud nation that has ever fallen already lies.
basic.typology: Like Nebuchadnezzar's tree in Daniel 4 and the fallen king pictured in Isaiah 14, the felled cedar previews every proud kingdom's descent into the pit. Christ is the deliberate reversal of this pattern: rather than grasping at heaven's height, He emptied Himself and humbled Himself to death, and it is for that humbling that God has highly exalted Him, Philippians 2:5-11.
basic.christ: This oracle indicts human pride at its most towering, the same pride the whole sequence against the nations has exposed since Tyre's prince tried to sit 'in the seat of gods', Ezekiel 28:2. Every cedar that climbs by its own strength is cut down. Christ alone climbs by the opposite path of humility and obedience even to the cross, and it is that path God exalts, giving Him the name above every name, Philippians 2:9-11.
basic.god: God is sovereign over every empire's rise and fall. The waters and deep springs that made the cedar great, verse 4, were His gift all along, so its pride was always a lie about the true source of its greatness. God opposes the proud precisely because pride forgets Him, and He alone decides when the ruthless nations He raises up will themselves be brought down.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 4:10-27 pictures the same truth in Nebuchadnezzar's tree vision. Isaiah 14:12-15 pronounces the same fall on a proud king who said 'I will ascend'. Proverbs 16:18 states the principle this whole allegory dramatizes. Philippians 2:5-11 shows Christ's deliberate reversal of the cedar's path.
basic.oneStory: This is the last movement of the oracles against Egypt: the tallest cedar in Eden's garden, admired by every nation, is felled for its pride and cast down to Sheol, and Pharaoh is warned he will share its fate. Every empire's proud climb ends the same way, until the one King who did not grasp at heaven's height, but humbled Himself all the way to the cross, is given the name above every name.

context.literary:
The chapter is a single sustained comparison, framed by two questions and an answer. Verse 2 asks Pharaoh, 'Who can be compared to your greatness?' and verse 18 asks again, 'Who then is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden?' The long middle is the reply: the one who was comparable, Assyria, is shown in a four stage story of growth, felling, mourning and descent, and the audience is told to see itself in the last stage.

The parable has a clear order. Verses 3 to 9 describe the tree in its glory, with the water that fed it, the birds and beasts that sheltered in it, and the envy of Eden. Verses 10 to 14 give the verdict in two parts, pride in verse 10 and the delivery to 'the ruler of the nations' in verse 11, followed by the aftermath of fallen branches and a purpose clause in verse 14. Verses 15 to 17 are a funeral scene, with the deep covered, the rivers held back, Lebanon in mourning and the other trees 'consoled' below. Verse 18 closes with the identification.

Two features give the poem its force. The first is the shift of speaker: verses 3 to 9 are a description in the narrator's voice, but verse 9 ends with God claiming the credit, 'I made it beautiful,' so the glory was always a gift. The second is the vertical axis. The words for height, clouds and tops rise through verses 3 to 10, and then the verbs of going down, descending to the Pit, the depths of the earth and Sheol, run through verses 14 to 18. The poem is built as a long climb and a longer fall.
context.historical:
The oracle is dated to the eleventh year, third month, first day, around June 587 BC, with Jerusalem under siege and Egypt's promised help proving useless. The comparison it draws is with Assyria, whose fall was recent memory. Nineveh had fallen to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, and the remnants of Assyrian rule were finished within a few years after. A nation that had dominated the Near East for centuries was gone within a generation, and Egypt had been Assyria's last ally, Pharaoh Neco marching north to help it in 609, 2 Kings 23:29. Ezekiel's hearers could remember when Assyria seemed immovable.

The imagery draws on the ancient world's habit of comparing kings to great trees. Lebanon's cedars were the standard of height and quality, used in Solomon's temple and in the palaces of kings, and the conquerors of Lebanon prided themselves on cutting them down. Isaiah 37:24 records the Assyrian king's own boast that he had cut down its tallest cedars, so the oracle turns the logger into the logged. The garden of God and the trees of Eden belong to the same mythic vocabulary Ezekiel used for Tyre in 28:13, and the poem treats Eden not as a map but as the standard of all that is glorious.

The 'ruler of the nations' of verse 11 and the 'foreigners, the most ruthless of the nations' of verse 12 refer to Babylon, which brought Assyria down. This makes the lesson sharper for the exiles' Babylonian masters as well, since the sequence of cedars did not end with Assyria.
context.canonical:
Trees are a constant Biblical picture of kings and kingdoms. Psalm 1:3 sets the righteous person as a tree planted by streams. Psalm 92:12 says the righteous grow 'like a cedar in Lebanon.' Ezekiel himself used the cedar in 17:3 to 4, in the story of the eagle that took off the topmost shoot, and again in 17:22 to 24, where God plants a shoot on a high mountain so that birds of every kind nest in its shade. Chapter 31 is the counter-parable: a tree that God did not plant that grows itself high.

The pride narrative is traced elsewhere in the prophets. Isaiah 2:12 to 13 says the Day of the LORD is against all the cedars of Lebanon, and Isaiah 10:33 to 34 says the Lord will clear the forest with an axe, so that Lebanon falls before the Mighty One. Zechariah 11:1 to 2 has the cedar fall and the cypress wail. In Daniel 4:10 to 22, the tree whose top reached the sky is Nebuchadnezzar himself, and the same chapter ends with the king learning that the Most High rules, Daniel 4:32. Isaiah 14:8 to 15 sets the felled cypresses and cedars rejoicing beside the king who 'said in your heart' that he would ascend and was brought down to Sheol, a close companion to Ezekiel 31:14 to 18.

The New Testament does not quote the chapter but summarises its law in the saying that whoever exalts himself will be humbled, Luke 18:14, and in Peter's reminder that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, 1 Peter 5:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's oracle was meant to disenchant Egypt. Pharaoh and his multitude felt secure because Egypt was great, and Judah looked at Egypt's size and saw safety. The prophet does not argue that Egypt is small. He grants that she is great, then asks who else was great, and answers with the greatest, Assyria, which God felled. The point is that greatness is not a shelter. It was not for Assyria and it will not be for Egypt.

He also wanted his hearers to understand where greatness comes from. The waters and the springs that made the tree tall, verse 4, and the God who says 'I made it beautiful,' verse 9, mean that nothing which grows high is self made. The pride lay in forgetting this. For exiles tempted to pin their hopes on one or another empire, the oracle trained them to see every empire as a tree watered from above and removed by the same hand.

The passage also has a pastoral edge. It records a real grief: God makes the deep mourn, the rivers stop, Lebanon mourns and the trees faint, verse 15. Even a proud power's fall is not told with glee. Ezekiel's hearers were meant to feel the weight of what happens when a people with such gifts misuses them, and to hear in it a warning to themselves.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a poem about what happened to Assyria and what will happen to Egypt. It is not a prescription that every tall tree must be felled, nor a commendation of the ruthless nations that wield the axe. Verse 12 calls the foreigners 'the most ruthless of the nations,' and the Bible elsewhere makes plain that such instruments are held accountable, Isaiah 10:15 and Habakkuk 2:8. The chapter describes how God deals with pride; it does not say that all success is pride or that all large institutions are doomed.

What it asks of present readers is a habit of self-examination at the point where their own gifts are greatest. The question 'Who can be compared to your greatness?' is dangerous to anyone who has been made tall by water they did not provide, and it applies to a person, a church or a business as much as a nation. The reply is not self-contempt but gratitude for what was given, together with the humility Jesus describes in Luke 18:14.

debates.question: Is the cedar Assyria or Pharaoh himself?

views.label: Assyria as a warning example
views.case: The Hebrew of verse 3 can be read 'Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon,' as the BSB has it. On this reading Assyria is a historical parallel offered to Pharaoh, and verse 18 closes with the identification of Pharaoh with the one who will share the same fate. The structure of question and comparison supports this, and it matches Ezekiel's pattern of using the fate of one nation as a warning for another.

views.label: A tree name, with the cedar standing for Egypt
views.case: Some interpreters have noticed that the Hebrew word for Assyria in verse 3 is close to a word for a kind of tree, and have proposed reading a tree name there. On that view the whole parable describes Pharaoh directly, a tree in Lebanon. The ancient versions are not uniform, and a text note is not given in the BSB. This reading is a possibility, but it is not needed, and the repeated verb for descent in verses 15 to 18, to Sheol with those who went down earlier, fits the sequel to Assyria's fall.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: A third view holds that the cedar is a figure flexible enough to carry both nations: the tree is Assyria in its history and Egypt in its destiny. The shared phrase 'Pharaoh and all his multitude' in verse 18 invites the reader to treat the story of one as the pattern of the other.

debates.bearing: In all three readings the lesson is the same: Pharaoh will go where the great tree went. The parable works best when Assyria is a real past example, which is what the dating and the history suggest.

debates.question: What is the 'consolation' of the trees in verse 16?

views.label: Grim comfort in company
views.case: The 'trees of Eden' that had stood by the great tree find comfort below in finding the mighty fallen with them. This echoes Isaiah 14:9 to 10, where the kings in Sheol say, 'You too have become weak, as we are.' It is the comfort of shared defeat, not of peace.

views.label: A real relief for those who had lived under it
views.case: The nations that sheltered in the tree's shade, verse 6, and then abandoned it, verse 12, may be relieved that the tyrant has gone. Nahum 3:19 says that all who hear the news of Assyria applaud its downfall.

debates.bearing: Both views refuse to romanticise either greatness or its collapse. The consolation of the dead is thin, and the relief of the living is born of cruelty endured, which says something about what Assyria's greatness had cost.

study.originalLanguages:
The cedar is erez, the great tree of Lebanon, and its shade is the Hebrew tsel. Shade is the ancient world's word for protection under a king. Isaiah 30:2 and 3 uses it of Egypt, when Judah sought 'refuge in Egypt's shade,' and Ezekiel 17:23 uses it of the shoot God would plant. In Ezekiel 31 the shade has a crowd under it: birds, beasts and 'all the great nations,' verse 6. The poem measures the greatness of a power by how many creatures it shelters, and then shows them leaving, verse 12, when the shade is gone.

The waters that make the tree grow come from the deep. The Hebrew word in verse 4 is tehom, the same word as 'the deep' in Genesis 1:2. The tree's source is the primeval water that God ordered at creation. When the tree falls, God says 'I covered the deep because of it,' verse 15, so the deep itself goes into mourning. The language ties the rise of an empire to the order of creation, so that its fall disturbs the world.

The verb of descent, yarad, 'to go down,' drives the second half of the poem. The nations are 'consigned to death, to the depths of the earth, among the mortals who descend to the Pit,' verse 14, and the trees descend to Sheol in verses 15 to 17. The Pit, bor in verse 14, is a hole in the ground, and in the language of Sheol it names the place where the dead lie. The use of the same verb in every verse of the descent gives the passage the sound of a staircase.

The divine claim of verse 9, 'I made it beautiful,' uses the verb asah, make, again, the same verb as Pharaoh's boast in 29:3. Pharaoh says 'I made it,' and God says 'I made it.' The comparison between the Nile that Pharaoh claimed and the cedar that God made is intended. The phrase 'garden of God,' gan elohim, in verses 8 and 9, is the garden of Genesis 2 and the mountain-garden of Ezekiel 28:13, and the trees 'of Eden' make the whole forest a sacred one.

The ending 'You will lie among the uncircumcised,' verse 18, uses arelim, the label that would sound shameful to a covenant ear, as Genesis 17:14 shows. For a proud Egyptian king, whose land Jeremiah 9:25 to 26 lists among the circumcised in the flesh, the phrase is a sharp reversal. The word reappears in chapter 32 and will be considered there.

typology.type: The great tree among the trees of Eden, Ezekiel 31:8 to 9
typology.fulfillment: A power so tall that Eden envied it, brought down for height of pride, is a shadow of the first fall, where the aim was to be like God, Genesis 3:5. Paul sees that the first Adam failed to receive what God gave, and the last Adam succeeded, Romans 5:19. Christ, who was in the form of God, did not grasp at equality, Philippians 2:6, and so was exalted. The pattern in Ezekiel is a repeated human failure; in Christ it is reversed. The type falls short in that the cedar is a nation while Christ is a person, and the tree is felled for its pride while Christ is lifted up for His obedience.

typology.type: The felled tree and the stump that does not sprout, Ezekiel 31:12 to 14
typology.fulfillment: The cedar is cut down, and no shoot is promised. Contrast the line of Jesse, from which 'a shoot will spring up from the stump,' Isaiah 11:1, where the felled tree gives life. Jesus says that unless a grain of wheat falls and dies it remains alone, but if it dies it bears much fruit, John 12:24. The pattern of Ezekiel is the cutting down of a tree with no future; Christ enters death and brings fruit. The type shows how a fall can be final, which is why the gospel sets the cross beside it, in a different direction.

typology.type: The shade of the tree where the nations lived, Ezekiel 31:6
typology.fulfillment: A kingdom is described as a tree where birds nest and beasts shelter. Jesus uses the same picture for the kingdom of God, which grows like a mustard seed until the birds of the air nest in its shade, Mark 4:32. Ezekiel 17:23 had already promised that God would plant a tree in Israel where birds of every kind would nest. The correspondence is of image, and the contrast is of origin: Assyria's tree grew from the great waters of its own power, the kingdom grows from a small seed that God plants. The type falls short because Jesus' kingdom is not defined by height.

typology.type: The descent to Sheol, Ezekiel 31:15 to 17
typology.fulfillment: Every tree descends to the pit, and no one returns. The New Testament says that Christ also descended to the lower parts of the earth, Ephesians 4:9, and that God did not abandon His soul to Hades, Acts 2:27, quoting Psalm 16:10. He now holds the keys of Death and Hades, Revelation 1:18. The type is the universal descent of the proud into death; the antitype is the single descent of the humble One who came back out. Where Ezekiel's trees go down to be consoled by company, Christ goes down to take the keys.

study.christ:
Christ does not appear in this chapter as a figure within it, and it would be a mistake to look for Him among the branches. The chapter prepares for Him by describing exactly what He is not and what He undoes.

The first connection is by contrast of paths. The tree grows high and its heart is lifted up, and God brings it down. Paul puts the opposite movement in a hymn: Christ, 'existing in the form of God,' did not grasp equality with God, but emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself and became obedient to death on a cross, and therefore God exalted Him, Philippians 2:6 to 9. Ezekiel's rule that God humbles the proud is turned into its twin: God exalts the humble. That is why Jesus can say that whoever exalts himself will be humbled and whoever humbles himself will be exalted, Matthew 23:12, and why He can act on that rule Himself.

The second connection is the descent. The language of going down to Sheol, the Pit and the depths of the earth is the language the New Testament uses for Christ's own death and burial. Ephesians 4:9 speaks of His descent to the lower parts of the earth, and Peter, quoting David, says that God would not abandon Him to Hades, Acts 2:27. What for Assyria and Egypt is an end is for Him a passage, and He now holds the keys, Revelation 1:18. Ezekiel's trees are 'consoled' by company in the grave; Christ breaks the grave open from within.

The third connection is the shade. The great nations sheltered under Assyria, and that shelter failed. The Gospel offers another shelter. Jesus says the kingdom grows from a mustard seed until the birds of the air nest in its shade, Mark 4:32, and He calls Himself the vine into which others are grafted, John 15:5. Where Assyria's tree drew the world beneath its power, the kingdom draws the world into His life.

The fourth is the Branch. Isaiah promised that from the stump of Jesse a shoot would spring up, Isaiah 11:1. A felled tree is not always finished. Ezekiel's cedar has no such promise, which is why its fall is a warning. The cut-down tree of David's line, in the death of Jesus, is the one stump from which life came.

A caution is needed. The chapter is not a coded sermon on the cross. It is a poem on pride and its end, and its relevance to Christ lies in the reversal that the New Testament sets against it.
study.god:
God appears first as the source of all greatness. 'I made it beautiful with its many branches,' verse 9, is a sentence that the proud tree never hears. The waters, the springs, the shade, the envy of Eden are His. The oracle asks the reader to see that what looks like the achievement of a nation is the gift of its Creator, and that the deep itself is at His command, since He can cover it and restrain its rivers, verse 15.

He is the Lord of nations who judges according to what has been done with the gift. Verse 11 says He delivered the tree 'into the hand of the ruler of the nations, for him to deal with it according to its wickedness.' The verdict is moral. It is not an accident of geography or military luck, and it is not capricious. The ruthless foreigners who cut the tree are instruments, and their own turn will come. The God who raises a power to height also decides its end.

He has a purpose in the fall that reaches beyond the tree. Verse 14 says it happened 'so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height.' God's judgment of one power is a lesson for the next, and the telling of it to Pharaoh is an act of patience: he is shown the pattern before he enters it. The God who judges also warns.

He is not indifferent. In verse 15 He says, 'I caused mourning.' The great deep is covered, the rivers are held back and Lebanon grieves. A judgment that moves the creation to mourning is a judgment that is not callous. The sovereign who fells the tree is the same Lord who makes the world sorrow for it, which fits Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11, where He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.

For worship, the chapter calls us to receive every gift as a gift, to bow where a tree would rise, and to praise the God who raises up and brings down. It also tells us that His warnings are mercy, since a tree that has seen the stump of another can still choose to bend.

crossReferences.note: Pharaoh says of the Nile, 'I made it myself.' Ezekiel 31:9 has God say of the cedar, 'I made it beautiful.' The two verses are meant to be heard together, since the same boast that Pharaoh makes about his river is answered by a claim from the real Maker.

God plants a shoot on a high mountain so that birds of every kind nest in its shade, and says He brings the tall tree down and makes the low tree tall. This is the positive counterpart to the felled cedar, and it states the principle behind Ezekiel 31 as God's own policy.

Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a tree whose top reached the sky, with beasts under it and birds in its branches, uses almost the same image as Ezekiel 31:3 to 6. Daniel 4:22 says the tree is the king, and verse 32 says the Most High rules.

The one who said 'I will ascend' is brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit. The pattern of climbing and descent, and the same vocabulary of Pit and Sheol, make this a close companion to Ezekiel 31:14 to 18.

The Day of the LORD is against all the proud and lofty, including the cedars of Lebanon. Isaiah gives the principle in plain prose that Ezekiel dramatises in a parable: the lofty will be humbled, and the cedar is the symbol of loftiness.

The Assyrian king boasts that he has cut down Lebanon's tallest cedars. Ezekiel's parable reverses the boast, since the great cedar is Assyria itself and others, the ruthless foreigners of verse 12, cut it down.

The way back to the tree of life is guarded east of Eden. Ezekiel's trees of Eden descend instead, and the shared imagery of Eden, garden of God and fall invites a link between the first human pride and the pride of empires.

Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. It is the one line summary of the parable, and it shows that Ezekiel's story belongs to the wisdom tradition as much as the prophetic.

Christ did not grasp equality with God but humbled Himself to death on a cross, and God exalted Him. It is the exact reversal of the cedar's path, and Paul's hymn shows what the true greatness the tree missed would look like.

God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, so humble yourselves under His mighty hand that He may exalt you in due time. The New Testament states as an exhortation what Ezekiel 31 shows as a story.

The tree of life stands on either side of the river with leaves for the healing of the nations. It answers the great tree's false shelter with a true one, and recalls the trees of Eden in a form no pride can fell.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible has a garden at both ends, and Ezekiel 31 stands in the middle of the long story between them. In Genesis 2:9 God makes every tree pleasing to the eye grow from the ground, and in the centre He places the tree of life. The trees of Eden are the picture of what He gives. In Genesis 3 humanity reaches for a different kind of greatness, to be like God, and is driven out, with cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. The felling of the great cedar in Ezekiel 31 is a late retelling of that fall, with empires in the place of Adam.

The story of redemption also uses trees. God plants Israel as a vine and a shoot, Ezekiel 17:22 to 23, and promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1. The Gospel of John records that the Son falls like a grain of wheat into the earth and rises with much fruit, John 12:24. The tree on which He hangs, and from which He is taken down, is the place where the pride of the first tree is dealt with. What Ezekiel's cedar could not do, the cross does: a tree brings down the one who exalted himself, and raises the humble.

As for what the passage sets up, it prepares the reader for the great reversal of Revelation. There the proud empires, Babylon among them, fall in a day, and the nations are healed by the leaves of the tree of life, Revelation 22:2. The trees of Eden that were envious of a cedar now stand on either side of a river that no one claims to have made. The people who go in are those who have washed their robes and have the right to the tree of life, Revelation 22:14.

In the new creation the question that Ezekiel asks Pharaoh, 'Who can be compared to your greatness?' is finally answered. No one can be compared to the greatness of God, and the glory and honour of the nations are brought into His city as gifts, Revelation 21:26. What was grasped by the proud is given to the humble.

quiz.q: What image does God use to describe Assyria's unrivaled greatness before its downfall?

options.text: A towering cedar in Lebanon, its top among the clouds, envied by every tree in Eden's own garden.
options.note: Verses 3-9 develop this image at length, unrivaled by any tree in the garden of God.

options.text: A vine spreading across every valley of the land.
options.note: The image is a cedar tree, not a vine; compare Ezekiel 19 and 17 for vine imagery elsewhere.

options.text: A lion prowling among the nations.
options.note: That image is used for Pharaoh in Ezekiel 32:2, not here.

options.text: A river overflowing its banks each spring.
options.note: Waters and rivers feature in the description, verse 4, but the central image itself is the cedar.

quiz.q: Why does God bring the great cedar down, according to verses 10-11?

options.text: Because it grew proud on account of its height, so God delivered it into the hand of a ruthless ruler.
options.note: Verse 10 states the cause plainly: pride at its own greatness.

options.text: Because foreign armies simply happened to be stronger.
options.note: Foreign armies do the cutting, verse 12, but the stated cause is the tree's own pride.

options.text: Because the waters that fed it ran dry.
options.note: The opposite is true; abundant waters made it great, verses 4-5, 7.

options.text: Because other trees in the forest conspired against it.
options.note: Other trees respond to its fall, verse 16, but they do not cause it.

quiz.q: What happened to the cedar's allies and the creatures that had sheltered in its shade once it fell?

options.text: They abandoned its fallen shade, and its allies among the nations went down with it to Sheol.
options.note: Verses 12 and 17 record both the abandonment and the allies' shared descent.

options.text: They immediately began replanting the forest around it.
options.note: No such renewal is described; the scene is one of mourning and ruin.

options.text: They helped prop the fallen trunk back upright.
options.note: The birds and beasts merely nest on its fallen trunk, verse 13; nothing is restored.

options.text: They were entirely unaffected by its downfall.
options.note: They are affected: they leave its shade, and its allies share its fate in Sheol.

quiz.q: What is the point of the whole allegory, stated plainly in verse 18?

options.text: Pharaoh and all his multitude will share the fallen cedar's fate, brought down among the uncircumcised slain by the sword.
options.note: Verse 18 names Pharaoh directly as the target of the entire parable.

options.text: Pharaoh would repent and be spared judgment.
options.note: No repentance or reprieve is offered; the verse pronounces the same fate on Pharaoh.

options.text: Egypt would form a lasting alliance with Assyria's successors.
options.note: The allegory is about shared judgment, not political alliance.

options.text: The allegory was told only for its literary beauty, with no application to Pharaoh.
options.note: The parable is beautifully told, but verse 18 makes its application to Pharaoh explicit.

quiz.q: What does this oracle reveal about human pride before God?

options.text: However great and admired, pride that forgets God ends in the pit; the higher the proud climb, the harder they fall under His judgment.
options.note: The whole chapter dramatizes this principle through the cedar's rise and ruin.

options.text: Pride is only a danger for kings and nations, not for ordinary people.
options.note: The principle is stated as a general pattern, echoed throughout Scripture for every heart, Proverbs 16:18.

options.text: Greatness itself, wherever it is found, is sinful and forbidden.
options.note: The tree's greatness was God's own gift, verse 4; the sin is pride that forgets the Giver, not greatness itself.

options.text: God is indifferent to pride, treating it as a private matter between individuals.
options.note: The opposite is shown: God actively judges pride and brings it down, verses 10-11.

questions: This cedar's height, shade, and beauty were all gifts, 'the waters made it grow', yet it took the credit for its own greatness. Where are you tempted to treat what God has given you as something you achieved on your own?

Every bird and beast that sheltered in the cedar's branches was scattered when it fell, and its allies went down with it. What are you sheltering under right now that cannot actually hold you up the way you hope?

Pharaoh was warned by watching another proud nation's fall, yet history shows he did not turn from his own pride. What warnings has God already placed in front of you that you have been slow to take seriously?

Christ took the opposite road from every cedar in this chapter: down instead of up, humility instead of height, and was exalted precisely because of it. Where this week could you choose His path over the world's?
The chapter ends by naming the real target of the whole allegory: 'this is Pharaoh'. If God named your own particular pride as plainly and directly as this, what would He call it?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew text names Assyria here, and most translations, including the BSB, keep this reading; some ancient versions differ, but the comparison functions the same way regardless, holding up history's mightiest tree as a warning to Egypt.
'The Pit' and 'Sheol' translate two related Hebrew terms for the realm of the dead, used together in this passage to underline how total and final the fall described really is.

'The uncircumcised' functioned in Israel's vocabulary as a term of disgrace for those outside the covenant; applying it to Egypt, whose own men were circumcised, is a deliberate insult tied to their shameful death alongside nations Israel considered unclean.
